thread.title: Alphabet Earnings: Beats Estimates, Shares Rise 4%

author: Jon Swartz
title: Alphabet Earnings: Beats Estimates, Shares Rise 4%
text:
By Jon Swartz July 23, 2018 5:07 p.m. ET Illustration: Tiernan Ray for Barron's Alphabet (GOOGL) on Monday rang up better-than-expected second-quarter results that sent shares up nearly 4.5% to $1,265.57 in after-hours trading.
[On Tuesday, the stock was up an additional 4% to $1,263.73.]
Google's parent company has lagged among its Faang brethren this year. Its shares, while up 14% and easily outpacing S&P 500 Index, are far behind Amazon.com (AMZN), Netflix (NFLX), and Facebook (FB), which set a 52-week intraday high Monday despite flaps with data-analytics firms over the handling of user information.
The Mountain View, Calif.-based company announced earnings per share of $11.75 on revenue of $32.7 billion.
Analysts polled by FactSet expected Alphabet to report per-share earnings of $9.66, excluding the impact of a $5.07 billion charge in connection with a European Commission fine alleging abuse of its dominant Android operating system. Including the fine, Alphabet's EPS was $4.54. It is appealing the ruling.
In the same quarter a year ago, Alphabet reported per-share earnings of $8.90, which excluded a $2.7 billion charge for another European fine.
Alphabet was expected to report revenue of $32.17 billion, according to a Thomson Reuters consensus estimate.
Investors are keen as to whether Google will be forced to alter the business model for mobile-software distribution to adhere with the EU fine, and what those long-terms costs will be. They are also likely to keep an eye on the impact of the recently passed General Data Protection Regulation law in Europe, and its impact on digital ad sales.
Alphabet's advertising remained strong, at $28 billion in the second quarter. Other revenue, which includes its cloud business and hardware, was $4.4 billion.
"We remain positive on the secular ad growth story driven by mobile and YouTube combined with generally better expense management and a more shareholder-friendly capital allocation approach," Susquehanna analyst Shyam Patil wrote in a note to clients Monday.
Another source of optimism is Waymo , Google's self-driving unit. It has logged 8 million miles on public roads, compared with 5 million in February, as it approaches commercial service this year, prompting Morgan Stanley analysts to expect Alphabet to creep closer to $1 trillion in market valuation.
Alphabet continued to plow money into capital expenditures such as data centers, underseas cables, and real estate. Its spending soared to $5.5 billion in the quarter, compared with $2.8 billion in the same quarter a year earlier. Company Chief Financial Officer Ruth Porat said the investments were necessary for the company to maintain an edge in machine learning and other future technologies.
Google's rate of R&D spending puts it on pace for $20 billion in its fiscal year, compared to $13.1 billion for Apple (AAPL) over the last 12 months .
